demographics.trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one

Threat.value: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
Being superalert or watchful or on guard
Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame

issues.item: Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
issues.explanation: For trauma involving the unexpected death of a loved one, a specific sense of danger from strangers is hard to reconcile unless there is additional trauma history not represented here. The other threat items reflect generalized hypervigilance, but this item implies an interpersonal-danger context that is not supported by the trauma type or by any trigger, memory, appraisal, or strategy items.

issues.item: Scanning for Danger: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger
issues.explanation: For trauma involving the unexpected death of a loved one, this threat profile is hard to reconcile clinically: all selected items imply persistent fear of immediate external physical danger, which fits assault/combat more than bereavement trauma. In isolation, bereavement-related PTSD can involve arousal, but a purely danger-scanning threat node without any accompanying memory, trigger, appraisal, or strategy content linking the threat to reminders of the loved one's death is not coherent here. This is also difficult to square with the formulation, which specifies no active edges; the threat items strongly imply linkage to triggers or trauma reminders, yet no such connected content is present.

vignette:
Linh Tran is a 31-year-old Vietnamese-American journalist, recently divorced, who presented for an initial clinical consultation following the sudden death of her younger brother, Minh, eight months ago. Minh, twenty-six years old and in apparently good health, collapsed without warning at a family gathering - a Lunar New Year celebration at their parents' home in San Jose - and was pronounced dead within the hour from an undetected cardiac arrhythmia. Linh had been standing only a few feet away when it happened. She had been laughing at something he said. She had watched his face change before he fell.

In the weeks that followed, Linh described moving through her days as though the world had been subtly rewired. The gathering had been so ordinary - the smell of her mother's phở, the noise of relatives overlapping one another in conversation, the particular quality of afternoon light through her parents' kitchen window - and then it was not ordinary at all, and nothing since has felt ordinary again. What unsettled her most in those early weeks was not grief in any form she had anticipated. It was something closer to alarm, a constant low-grade vigilance that she could not locate a reason for and could not switch off.

That vigilance has since become one of the defining textures of her daily life. Linh described being perpetually watchful in a way that she finds both exhausting and, in some part of her, entirely logical. She had come to believe, in a way she could not fully articulate but could not argue herself out of, that the world contains sudden catastrophes that give no warning and that the only reasonable response is to remain alert to them at all times. At her desk in the newsroom, she finds herself scanning the room between sentences - not for anything specific, but scanning nonetheless. She monitors her colleagues' faces for signs of distress. She notices exits. She keeps her phone face-up and volume on at all times, and she has told herself this is professional habit, though she knows it is not.

Even in moments that should offer rest - her apartment in the evenings, a quiet Sunday morning - Linh cannot settle. She described lying on her couch after filing a story, aware on some level that she is safe, and yet finding her body unwilling to accept that information. Her jaw stays tight. Her attention keeps moving. She had come to believe that relaxing was a kind of carelessness, that Minh had been laughing, had been completely at ease, and then he was gone, and so ease itself had come to feel like a form of exposure to something she could not name.

The emotional weight she carries is not uniform. There is fear - the ambient, structureless kind - but layered beneath it are surges of horror when the memory of his face surfaces unexpectedly, and a guilt that she returns to with particular intensity. She had been the older sibling. She is certain, in the way that grief can manufacture certainty, that she should have seen something, noticed something, done something, even though every rational part of her knows there was nothing to see. The shame compounds this: shame at having laughed in the moment before, shame at having been helpless, shame at not knowing how to be a daughter to her parents in the months since, when her own distress has made her withdraw from them rather than draw closer.

Her work as a journalist has been directly affected. She covers local government and civic affairs, but in recent months her editor has twice asked her to take on human-interest stories involving sudden loss - an accident, a family in crisis - and both times Linh has quietly redirected the assignment to a colleague, offering scheduling conflicts as cover. She has not told anyone at the paper what happened to Minh.

What finally brought her to seek help was a phone call from her mother last month, gently noting that Linh seemed far away. Linh had no answer for her. She is most afraid, she said at intake, that she will feel like this indefinitely - watchful and guilty and unable to rest - and most hoping that someone can help her understand why she cannot simply grieve her brother the way she imagines grief is supposed to work.
